2611.28207.abstract: We present the detection of the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect for TOI-1333 Ab, a short-period gas giant ($P=4.72$ days) orbiting one component of a wide stellar binary (570 AU). Planets in wide binary systems like TOI-1333 Ab offer an opportunity to not only test for alignment between the planet's orbit and the star's spin, but also the orbit of the binary companion. We use radial velocity observations from the Tillinghast Reflector Echelle Spectrograph (TRES) to measure an aligned projected spin/orbit angle of the system $\lambda = 7.74^\circ \pm 20.70^\circ$. However, the inclination of the wide binary companion shows a significant misalignment (likely more than $\approx 30^\circ$) with the planet's orbit, which makes understanding the formation of the system challenging. We propose three different explanations for TOI-1333 Ab's unusual architecture, but cannot confidently distinguish between them. Ultimately, more observations of similar systems are needed in order to understand how hot Jupiters in binary systems form, evolve, and impact their stars.

2611.28471.abstract: Planet Nine is hypothesized to exist in the outer solar system in order to explain the physical orbital clustering of several trans-Neptunian objects. A Planet Nine would systematically change the location of the solar system barycenter (SSB). Therefore, the precise timing properties of millisecond radio pulsars would measure the acceleration, jerk, and snap of the currently-perceived SSB under the gravitational influence of a Planet Nine. We present a method on how to use pulsar spin frequency derivatives and binary pulsar orbital period derivatives to constrain the Planet Nine parameter space. We find that searches for unidentified massive objects in the solar system require at least cubic and quartic variations in the pulse times of arrival (corresponding to jerk and snap, respectively) in order to uniquely constrain an orbit. Otherwise, additional assumptions are required to fully constrain the mass and orbital parameters of the object. We use our method to weigh the ice giants Uranus and Neptune and obtain results consistent with the literature. This method could be used to weigh a Planet Nine after a putative optical detection. Future work will use updated pulsar timing datasets that benefit from longer observational baselines and advances in statistical modeling and noise characterization.

2611.28818.abstract: Confirmed and candidate planets in the Habitable or near-Habitable Zones (HZ) orbiting Sun-like stars are crucial not only for the search for life beyond the Solar System, but also for understanding the architecture and formation of other solar systems and for conducting demographic studies. Current analyses of such planetary systems are limited both by the small sample size revealed by Kepler as well as by uncertainties in system parameters. Although a larger sample of HZ and near-HZ planets must await new observations from wide-field, space-based surveys, follow-up analyses and observations with existing facilities can improve the precision on stellar and planetary parameters, enable more accurate planetary classification, and a more reliable assessment of whether candidate systems are true planets or merely astrophysical false positives. Here, we present a homogeneous transit light curve analysis of 187 HZ and near-HZ systems discovered by Kepler. Our analysis incorporates the latest Gaia DR3-derived stellar parameters, and we also present a statistical validation effort for all targets. The result is a uniform set of planetary radii, instellation fluxes, and orbital ephemerides suitable for prioritizing and scheduling follow-up observations to improve our understanding of planets in this regime. We show that longer-period (>300days) systems would particularly benefit from transit follow-up: just a single transit from facilities such as the 6m James Webb or the planned 3m Lazuli space telescopes could provide ~2 times tighter precision on planet radii than four years of Kepler photometry, thereby dramatically shrinking relevant parameter uncertainties and allowing more confident planet/false-positive assessments.

2611.28918.abstract:
Automated pipelines and machine-learning algorithms are efficient at detecting standard planetary transits, but can miss subtle, non-periodic morphological anomalies. We present the pilot phase of DIPS-OjOS (Detecting Irregular Photometric Signals - OjímetrO Survey), a professional-amateur collaboration designed to develop and validate a scalable workflow for identifying irregular photometric signals in exoplanet transit light curves through trained visual inspection. The project targets starspot-crossing events, stellar flares, circumplanetary structures, exomoon-like signatures, and transit-duration or timing anomalies overlooked by automated searches.
We built the infrastructure required for a controlled visual-inspection experiment: simulated control light curves, preparation and detrending of real short-cadence Kepler data, a transit-modeling pipeline that computes an optimized average transit profile for each light curve, and a web-based classification platform. The real sample was deliberately restricted to 51 well-characterized Kepler systems. Collaborators inspected 917 transit events: 555 real transits and 362 simulated controls. The simulated sample quantified observer performance and calibrated a weighted consensus scheme; collaborators recovered injected signals with an average efficiency of 87.6%, while the null-case false-positive rate was 15.3%.
After expert validation, we retained 88 viable candidate anomalies from the real sample, including 26 starspot-crossing event candidates across eight targets, seven stellar flares, 31 systematic transit-duration deviations motivating refined orbital parameters in four systems, and a mutual transit event in Kepler-89. Recovering candidate signals in this well-studied sample validates the sensitivity of DIPS-OjOS and establishes the basis for future applications to Kepler, TESS, PLATO, and ground-based datasets.

2611.29816.abstract: Stellar flybys can significantly alter the orbital configurations of planetary systems, potentially displacing planets initially located within the habitable zone (HZ) of their host stars. In this study, we investigate the dynamical effects of stellar encounters on HZ planets using a large suite of three-body N-body simulations. We examine how the properties of the host star, passing star, planetary orbit, and encounter geometry influence the final orbital configuration. A planet is considered to retain an HZ orbit only if it remains bound to its original host and its entire final orbital range, from periastron to apastron, lies within the HZ boundaries. Based on the simulation results, we develop an XGBoost classifier to predict the final HZ status of planets following stellar encounters. The model achieves an accuracy of 0.90, an ROC-AUC of 0.97, and a PR-AUC of 0.97 on the test set. Feature importance analysis identifies the encounter-impulse parameter as the dominant predictor of the outcome. The classifier provides a computational speedup of approximately 74 compared with direct N-body simulations. We further evaluate the model using an independent dataset representing a globular-cluster environment, where approximately 20 per cent of planets retain HZ orbits. Despite the naturally imbalanced class distribution, the model achieves an accuracy of 0.87, an ROC-AUC of 0.92, and a PR-AUC of 0.77. These results demonstrate the potential of machine learning for efficiently predicting the dynamical retention of HZ planets following stellar encounters and for investigating their outcomes in dense stellar environments.

2611.30136.abstract: Ultra-hot Jupiters allow simultaneous measurements of volatile molecules and refractory metals, providing constraints on atmospheric chemistry and refractory-element sequestration. We reanalyze the previously published Gemini-N/IGRINS-2 dayside emission spectra of WASP-33~b, extending the analysis to neutral refractory species. Using cross-correlation (CC) and likelihood-based (LL) detection methods, we recover the strongest species detection signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) from CO ($\rm CC~S/N=5.29,\ LL~S/N=5.62$). \ion{Mg}{1} ($\rm CC~S/N=3.88,\ LL~S/N=4.73$) and OH ($\rm CC~S/N=3.88,\ LL~S/N=3.89$) are recovered at lower significance in both metrics. H$_2$O remains marginal, appearing only in the cross-correlation analysis ($\rm CC~S/N=3.24$), while \ion{Ti}{1} ($\rm LL~S/N=3.70$) and \ion{Ca}{1} ($\rm LL~S/N=2.98$) show tentative signals. We do not detect \ion{Fe}{1}, \ion{Si}{1}, and \ion{V}{1} in this dataset. A chemical-equilibrium retrieval with a flexible Bezier-spline pressure--temperature profile yields ${\rm C/O}=0.65^{+0.09}_{-0.10}$ and $[{\rm M/H}]=-0.48^{+0.24}_{-0.18}$, and a refractory-to-volatile ratio of $[R/V]_{\rm p}=-0.15^{+0.24}_{-0.23}$. The corresponding stellar-normalized value is $[R/V]_{\rm p/ \star}=0.37^{+0.38}_{-0.36}$, but this value is sensitive to the stellar oxygen abundance. We find that the atmospheric Ti/Mg and Ca/Mg ratios of WASP-33~b are consistent with their respective stellar values within 68\% confidence. This is in contrast to other ultra-hot Jupiters with lower equilibrium temperatures that often show depleted Ti abundances compared to other metals, indicative of cold-trapping. This would suggest that even the nightside of WASP-33~b is too hot for significant condensation and sequestration to occur. Comparison with disk-chemistry models remains exploratory because the carbon-to-refractory posterior overlaps several formation scenarios.

2611.30158.abstract: The snow line location provides important constraints on rocky planet formation. Recent magnetohydrodynamical simulations suggest that Joule heating associated with gas accretion is so inefficient that the snow line can be located inside 1 au around a solar-type star. This challenges in-situ formation of the terrestrial planets in the solar system unless other internal heating processes are present. Previous studies have proposed that spiral shocks induced by an embedded planet potentially shift the snow line outward. In this study, we investigate the impact of shock heating induced by a giant planet on the location of the snow line in two steps. First, we perform two-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of a disk with a giant planet to model shock heating rates. We construct an empirical formula for total entropy jumps due to multiple spiral shocks interior to the planetary orbit. Second, we calculate the radial temperature profile based on the thermal balance with the modeled shock heating rates. We find that shock heating can substantially increase the disk temperature in inner regions far from the planet when the planetary mass and disk optical depth are sufficiently high. For example, assuming a fixed surface density profile and an opacity of $\kappa = 1~\rm cm^2\,g^{-1}$, a planet with one-third of Jupiter's current mass at 5 au can shift the snow line outward beyond 1 au. Our results suggest that the early formation of proto-Jupiter in the solar nebula may have enabled rocky planetesimals and protoplanets to form in the present-day terrestrial planet region without invoking additional water removal processes.

2611.30331.abstract: Centimetre-sized meteoroids released by the active asteroid (3200) Phaethon, parent of the Geminid meteor shower, probe the ejection of refractory material from a comet-asteroid transition object and the age of the stream; lunar impact flashes (LIFs) are the only ground-based technique that samples this size range. We determine the impact flux, mass and size distributions, and expected crater sizes of Geminid meteoroids on the Moon from campaigns at the 2018 and 2025 maxima, and test the stability of the centimetre-sized population over seven years. Both campaigns used the Nihon University 0.40 m "GUNDAM" telescope with CMOS video cameras at 60 fps, with candidates validated at independent stations; a common aperture-photometry pipeline calibrated in the Cousins R band gave peak magnitudes to 0.1-0.25 mag. Eleven LIFs were detected in 3.3 h in 2018 and nine in 2.2 h in 2025, all with Geminid probabilities of 0.87-0.96. With monitored areas measured on the video frames, the campaigns give consistent fluxes of $4.2\times10^{-7}$ and $5.2\times10^{-7}$ km$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$ (merged: $4.6\times10^{-7}$ km$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$). For a luminous efficiency of $1.4\times10^{-3}$ the impactors have masses of 10-320 g, diameters of 1.8-5.9 cm, and predicted crater rim diameters of 2-5 m. The combined sample gives a maximum-likelihood mass index $s=1.76\pm0.17$ and a population index $r=2.0\pm0.3$, markedly shallower than the NELIOTA all-flash values; a single power law with this slope connects the Global Meteor Network millimetre flux to the LIF centimetre flux. The Geminid stream delivers an excess of large particles relative to the sporadic background, consistent with an asteroidal origin, and its stable centimetre-sized flux over seven years constrains stream-formation models with ages of $2\times10^3$-$2\times10^4$ yr.

2611.30459.abstract: On March 12, 2025, Hera, the European Space Agency's planetary defense mission, performed a Mars flyby en route to the asteroid system (65803) Didymos-Dimorphos. During this event, HyperScout-H (HS-H), the spacecraft's hyperspectral imager, acquired five high spatial resolution images over the southern hemisphere of Mars. These observations provide an opportunity for systematic cross-calibration of HS-H with two established Mars orbital instruments, Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) on board the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (Murchie et al., 2007), and Observatoire pour la Minéralogie, l'Eau, les Glaces et l'Activité (OMEGA) on board Mars Express (Bibring et al., 2004). This study evaluates the performance, reliability, and readiness of HS-H for the forthcoming asteroid observation phase by comparing it with CRISM and OMEGA data. We selected 21 surface regions spanning diverse terrain types from three HS-H images in which the Martian surface fills the entire field of view. These images were corrected, calibrated, and co-registered to associate each pixel with latitude and longitude. The relative inter-channel correction factors are close to unity for bands 3-25 (0.688-0.952 {\mu}m), with standard deviations of 0.52% for OMEGA and 0.62% for CRISM, indicating good agreement in spectral shape. Bands 1 and 2 show a systematic mismatch of 4.7% and 3.6%. The absolute flux correction factors reveal offsets of 8% relative to OMEGA and approximately 0.7% relative to CRISM, with mean inter-image standard deviations below 2%. These results confirm the radiometric stability of HS-H and establish a calibration framework for future Didymos-Dimorphos observations.

2611.30855.abstract: Warm Jupiters are, on average, more closely aligned with their host stars than hot Jupiters, even at high eccentricities. The low projected obliquities of eccentric warm Jupiters on the tidal migration track are difficult to reconcile with high-eccentricity migration (HEM) pathways that excite large misalignments. We examine whether tides acting on the star can realign initially misaligned systems before their orbits circularize. We extend a frequency-dependent tidal model to arbitrary eccentricities and focus on the $(1,0)$ obliquity tide. This component is stationary in the inertial frame, dissipates stellar rotational energy, and can change spin obliquity while leaving the semimajor axis and eccentricity unchanged. Its forcing frequency in the stellar rotating frame coincides with that of the rigid spin-over mode, which is non-dissipative. The strength of dissipation by non-rigid motions at this same frequency remains uncertain. In our models, enhancing the dissipative response by a factor of $10^7$ produces appreciable obliquity damping for Jupiter-mass planets. The stronger damping for more massive planets suggests that an enhancement of $10^6$ may suffice for super-Jupiters. Realignment can outpace circularization if the planet is already on an eccentric warm orbit while the star is still inflated and rapidly rotating during the pre-main sequence (PMS). If alignment occurs then, present-day stellar effective temperature may be a weak predictor of obliquity. In binary-driven HEM runs initialized at the zero-age main sequence, orbital circularization outpaces realignment in systems with sustained eccentricity forcing. The stellar quadrupole scaling suggests substantially stronger suppression of eccentricity excitation for PMS starts. These results cast doubt on binary-driven HEM as the origin of such aligned eccentric warm Jupiters, even when they lie along the tidal migration track.

2611.31057.abstract: We perform a joint analysis of ground-based radial velocities (RVs), Hipparcos Intermediate Astrometric Data, and two-epoch Gaia astrometry for known M dwarfs hosting cold Jupiters discovered through long-term spectroscopic monitoring. Among a sample of 25 planets in 19 systems, we derive robust absolute masses and orbital solutions for 13 planets in 11 systems with companion inclination uncertainties lower than 30 degrees. These include first mass measurements for five planets: GJ 328b, GJ 649b, GJ 849b and c, and GJ 9066c. We also reclassify one object, HIP 79431B, as a brown dwarf. We further compare the mass ratios of these 13 cold Jupiter systems with those of giant planets orbiting M stars characterized via transit, microlensing, and direct imaging. Without correcting for detection bias, we find that (1) there is likely a deficiency of high-mass-ratio hot Jupiters around M dwarfs compared with cold Jupiters, and (2) the local cold Jupiters orbiting M stars found by RV observations exhibit a similar mass ratio distribution as the counterparts in the Galactic bulge found by microlensing. Cold Jupiters orbiting stars with masses above $0.65~M_\odot$ tend to be more massive than those around M dwarfs. Our study establishes a sample of local cold Jupiters with precise mass determinations around M dwarfs, and reveal a tip of the iceberg in the upcoming Gaia DR4 and DR5.

Green bars meet the adopted closure criterion (interval half-width below 0.05); red bars do not. The stricter full-width reading (interval width below 0.05) is met by 9 of the 10 leading rocky parameters at each threshold, 7 and 8 of 10 for the combined branch, and 2 and 3 of 10 for the Hycean branch, at $5\sigma$ and $3\sigma$ respectively; the full widths for the rocky branch are listed in Table 3. 2611.31181.abstract: Deciding which temperate exoplanets to observe first matters for JWST transit spectroscopy and for planned ELT reflected-light instruments, yet signal-to-noise metrics ignore habitability and similarity indices ignore observability. We present an open Monte Carlo framework (UHI v6.1) that builds probabilistic priority lists separately for each facility and composition class, never as a single ranking. For each of 6,112 planets in the NASA Exoplanet Archive, 10,000 draws carry catalogue uncertainties through climate, cumulative stellar-XUV atmospheric retention, per-draw rocky, Hycean or gas-rich classes, and a JWST (transiting) or ELT/PCS (non-transiting) detection model, giving each planet a survival probability, a conditional score and a top-N probability. At $5\sigma$, 255 rocky and 71 Hycean candidates remain viable. A Saltelli--Sobol analysis of 32 assumptions ($N = 512$) shows that the location and width of the XUV shoreline dominate the rocky lists, with total-order indices of 0.22 and 0.12 at $5\sigma$ (0.25 and 0.14 at $3\sigma$), and all ten leading indices have 95% bootstrap half-widths below 0.05. For Hycean planets most outputs are degenerate and the analysis does not converge, so that branch is reported as indicative. Membership of these lists is limited mainly by whether a planet survives the habitability vetoes: at $5\sigma$, 3 of the nominal JWST and 4 of the nominal ELT rocky top-10 targets enter the top 10 in at least half of all draws, yet every one of them stays in the top 10 in more than half of the draws in which it survives. Code, per-planet posterior summaries, sensitivity tables and maps are public, so observers can rerun the lists under their own instrument assumptions and see which inputs would most change a target's priority.

2611.28189.abstract: Spaceborne remote sensing of the cryosphere is fundamental to map ice structure and dynamics. Accurate mass balance estimation requires a better understanding of melt/refreeze processes and firn hydrology, whereas spaceborne optical and Radar sensors are mostly limited to near-surface observations. The BIOMASS P-band Synthetic Aperture Radar, launched by European Space Agency in 2025, provides an unprecedented opportunity to gain a more direct access to englacial processes, thanks to the 70 cm wavelength paired with polarimetry, interferometry and tomography. This paper investigates subsurface beneath a region of historical supraglacial lake activity with BIOMASS tomography, at the Riiser-Larsen Ice Shelf in East Antarctica. The main result is that subsurface scattering appears to be related to historical supraglacial lake recurrence, with structural and depth variations over time. This suggests that recurrent supraglacial lake activity may leave persistent hydrological signatures within the firn. Overall, this study highlights the potential of gaining valuable insights into ice sheet hydrology with P-band.

2611.28537.abstract: Most stars in the field are part of binary, triple, or higher-order systems, which we primarily observe in hierarchical configurations that allow long-term stability. Over long timescales, hierarchical triple systems interact primarily through gravitational dynamics, but more complex interactions arise when stellar evolution drives mass transfer. In this paper, we study tertiary mass transfer in hierarchical triple systems using three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations. We find that the finite separation of the inner binary produces oscillations in the Roche potential that critically alter both the donor star's variability and its mean mass-loss rate. For compact inner binaries, the mass-loss rate approaches that of a single accretor, while at larger separations the orbit-averaged mass-loss rate increases steeply, approximately as $\langle \dot{M}_d\rangle \propto \langle \dot{M}_{d,0}\rangle (1+C a_b^{6.1 \pm 0.9})$. For the $\gamma = 5/3$ polytropic donor considered here, this scaling is consistent with the nonlinear response of Roche-lobe overflow to the leading quadrupolar perturbation of the inner-binary potential, which scales as $\delta\Phi_2 \propto a_b^2$. We also examine the donor's response to periodic forcing from the inner binary and find a transition between individual and collaborative accretion that determines whether the transferred material can form and sustain a circumbinary disk. Our results show that the finite separation of the inner binary can strongly regulate both the rate and fate of tertiary mass transfer, constraining a poorly understood phase of hierarchical triple evolution.

2611.28728.abstract: Designing low-thrust multi-asteroid rendezvous missions requires the coupled selection of asteroid sequences, encounter epochs, and low-thrust trajectories. Lambert transfers support rapid beam search but do not directly describe thrust-limited transfer capacity or propellant consumption. This paper develops two complementary low-thrust neural approximators. The first directly predicts the continuous maximum admissible initial mass from numerically optimized low-thrust transfers, providing a transfer-capacity estimate for comparison with the current spacecraft mass. The second predicts mass-dependent propellant consumption and propagates spacecraft mass to subsequent legs. With the carefully-designed input features and network structure, the approximators reduce mean absolute errors by 72.2% and 75.5%, respectively, relative to conventional deep neural network baselines. These predictions are incorporated into a Lambert-ranked beam search through resource filtering and recursive mass propagation before final beam selection. The method is evaluated on fixed-visit, maximum-visit, and deployment-collection missions. Across the tested cases, the proposed resource filtering increases the fraction of candidate sequences that yield accepted low-thrust solutions, raises the maximum validated asteroid-visit count by up to 15.4%, and improves the best mission objective by up to 17.8%. These results demonstrate that continuous transfer-capacity and propellant predictions can improve finite-width sequence search.

2611.28969.abstract: We validate a subset of the astrometric accelerations reported in Gaia DR3 non-single-star solutions by their consistency with the gravitational pull of known, resolved companions. Cross-matching 338,215 DR3 acceleration solutions against the Washington Double Star (WDS) catalog of visual binaries yields 2,466 unique pairs within 2". For each pair we compare the measured acceleration with alpha_max, the Newtonian bound on the acceleration the companion can impart on the Gaia-tracked photocenter. For 98.1% of the pairs the measured acceleration exceeds this bound by more than a factor of 10, so the cataloged companion cannot be responsible and the perturber must be a closer, unresolved one. The remaining 45 plausible wide binaries are close pairs at the WDS resolution limit. We fit orbits with an updated orvara, extended to accept the DR3 acceleration and jerk coefficients as direct constraints and released with htof as part of this work. The fits converge for 16 of the 45 and one boundary case, the rest having too few resolved measures or a perturber other than the cataloged pair, and 13 of the 17 carry enough data to test the coefficients. Eleven of the 13 statistically accommodate the reported accelerations, for seven- and nine-parameter solutions alike, and the dynamical companion masses agree with the photometric estimates where the photocenter conversion is well determined. Independently of the fits, 33 of the 43 plausible systems with a usable position angle (77%) have the acceleration directed within 45 degrees of the primary-companion axis, against 50% for a control sample: DR3's measured accelerations point in the directions of the cataloged companions.

S1: A two-stage training strategy separates synthetic pre-training data (MCD v6.1) from observational fine-tuning sources (EMARS, OpenMARS; with TES/MCS as the underlying retrievals); intervention actions at enter the transition model as continuous vectors. S2: A state encoder maps atmospheric fields to a latent $z$; PINN constraints and UDE residuals regularize the latent and downstream dynamics, merged at the concatenation node. S3: An RSSM propagates stochastic latent $z_{t}$ and recurrent memory $h_{t}$ under action-conditioned transitions $\rho(z\mid h,a)$ with physics enforced at every step; $h_{t}$ is updated from $(h_{t-1},z_{t-1},a_{t-1})$ via the recurrent backbone. S4: An actor-critic head trains within imagined latent rollouts; the actor $\pi(a\mid z,h)$ outputs intervention policies, the critic $V(z,h)$ estimates returns from $(\Delta P,\Delta T,\Delta O_{2})$, and a decoder reconstructs gridded fields against EMARS as an auxiliary signal. S5: Outputs are a learned policy trajectory, a long-horizon atmospheric forecast, and a rollout uncertainty map from stochastic latent samples.

2611.29856.abstract: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.

2611.30451.abstract: Determining M dwarf ages remains challenging because of their slow main-sequence evolution. We investigate using transiting brown dwarfs to constrain system ages through their measured masses and thermal emission. We report Palomar/WIRC secondary-eclipse observations of two close-in brown dwarfs, LP 261-75C and AD 3116B, measuring eclipse depths of $6.1 \pm 0.3$ parts per thousand (ppt) in $K_s$ and $9.1 \pm 0.6$ ppt in $J$, respectively. Combining these observations with space-based transit photometry, radial velocities, and host star spectra, we infer brown dwarf internal luminosities and, assuming coevality, host star ages using five sets of atmospheric and evolutionary models. For LP 261-75C, model-dependent median ages span 1.3-2.9 Gyr, substantially older than the previously proposed age of 0.1-0.2 Gyr based on presumed membership in the AB Doradus moving group. This result, the host star's high metallicity, and the companion's measured radius disfavor AB Dor membership. The revised age implies a mass of $\approx 62$-$68$ $M_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ for the wide-orbit companion LP 261-75B, compared with an earlier estimate of $\approx 21$ $M_{\mathrm{Jup}}$. AD 3116B, a member of the 0.6-0.8 Gyr Praesepe cluster, provides a test of brown dwarf evolutionary models through independent constraints on its mass, age, and luminosity. Its inferred age depends strongly on cloud treatment, spanning 0.4-0.6 Gyr for cloudy models and 1.0-1.3 Gyr for cloudless models. Among the models considered, Sonora Diamondback, which includes cloud condensation and cloud clearing across the L/T boundary, provides a plausible simultaneous match to the observed eclipse depth and radius. These results demonstrate a new method to constrain M dwarf ages using emission observations of their brown dwarf companions, while highlighting the sensitivity of the inferred temperatures and ages to evolutionary model differences.
